newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Fokker receivers play down relaunch hopes - paper.
newsitem.headline: Fokker receivers play down relaunch hopes - paper.

text.p: The administrators of bankrupt Dutch aircraft maker Fokker NV are not encouraging hopes that the company can be saved, Dutch newspaper Financieele Dagblad said on Saturday.
"All the fuss in the reporting over the chances of survival is completely overdone," the paper reported the receivers' spokesman Ben Knueppe as saying.
At the same time, however, Knueppe said that the receivers were still prepared to consider any viable plan, although time was clearly running out.
"Anyone who presents themselves now with a well-formulated plan and a large sack of money can do business," he said.
No-one at the receivers was available for comment on Saturday.

News this week that that Dutch industrial groups Stork and Begemann were in discussions over Fokker's future once again roused media interest. Stork bought Fokker's profitable maintenance and aircraft component operations last year.
Dutch newspaper Algemeen Dagblad said on Thursday the discussions, which also involved a large Singaporean finance company, had reached a critical stage and had already lined up 400 million guilders.
On Friday, Dutch Premier Wim Kok said the government was pleased with the developments and would seriously consider any rescue package.

"It is a good thing that another chance has come. It is our intention to fully investigate this possibility... It is the Netherlands' intention to grab any new opportunities for Fokker, if they come," he said.
However, the prospects of a Fokker rescue have become steadily more remote since the company was declared bankrupt in March last year.
In November, one of its key suppliers, Shorts, a unit of Canada's Bombardier Group, decided to close down production of wings for the Fokker F-70 and F-100 regional jets.
The Algemeen Dagblad reported on Thursday that Begemann president Andre Deleye had reached agreement with Shorts to resume production and had landed pre-orders for 35 new aircraft.
Back in November, the same newspaper declared that: "All hope for Fokker has flown".
In December, Fokker's principal suitor, Korea's Samsung Aerospace, pulled out of negotiations over a rescue bid.
Russian plane-maker Yakovlev has since repeated its interest in taking over Fokker, but the Dutch have doubts about its ability to finance such a deal.
